title: The 158-Year-Old Bank That Died in a Weekend
hook: Lehman Brothers survived the Civil War, the Great Depression and two world wars. It did not survive three days in September 2008.
body:
It started as a dry goods shop in Montgomery, Alabama in 1844, where the customers paid in cotton because they had no money -- and Henry Lehman sold the cotton on. A hundred and fifty-eight years later his firm was doing exactly the same thing with American mortgages, at more than thirty dollars borrowed for every one it owned. This is how Lehman Brothers turned houses into bonds, how Repo 105 moved up to $50 billion off its balance sheet a few days before every quarter closed, how David Einhorn read the whole thing out loud on a stage in May 2008, and how three days at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York ended with the largest bankruptcy in American history: $639 billion in assets, $613 billion in debt, 25,000 employees, and cardboard boxes on Seventh Avenue.

SOURCES: Report of Anton R. Valukas (Lehman bankruptcy examiner, 2010); FCIC Final Report ch.18; SEC EDGAR filings (Lehman FY2007 10-K, 8-K of 2008-09-10); House Oversight Committee hearing, 2008-10-06; David Einhorn, "Accounting Ingenuity", Ira W. Sohn conference, 2008-05-21; Encyclopedia of Alabama and the HBS Baker Library Lehman exhibit for the Montgomery origin. Every figure used is listed with its source in the production notes.

For educational and entertainment purposes. Historical events are dramatised; no dialogue in this video is presented as a verbatim quotation.
pinned: The part that still gets me: none of it was secret. The leverage was in the filings, the mortgages were in the newspapers, and David Einhorn read Lehman's own numbers out loud on a stage on May 21st, 2008 -- four months before the bankruptcy. Which number in this one surprised you most?
